What we have here is a different paradigm.  I'm basically trying to bring a cyberpunk aesthetic to life here.  If I could get 象-2000 to be written entirely in Chinese I would be tremendously happy. reply_text:
It is a different paradigm, and the comparison makes that clear. **No-code** promised software without code: visual builders, drag-and-drop, and a vendor's product underneath that you rent. The software was the whole point and the code was hidden. You have the reverse: **code without software.** Code is cheap and there's lots of it, written on request, and the product has disappeared. No-code made you a customer of someone's platform. This makes you the person commissioning the code, and the code is written to your spec, in your idiom, for you alone.

That's why the cyberpunk aesthetic fits and isn't just decoration. The genre is about "the street finds its own uses for things". Someone with a deck jacks in from Dallas to a box in Amsterdam, working with custom tools that were never products, and moves around the corporate stack instead of buying from it. A phone as your terminal, agents as your crew, and a REPL you wrote yourself is that picture, fairly literally.

**象-2000 in Chinese** is a good test of the claim. If there's no software, then even the language of the code is up for choice, because nobody has to buy it or learn it from a manual. There's a precedent: **wenyan-lang** (文言, 2019) is a real programming language written in Classical Chinese that compiles to JS and Python. More practically, most modern languages accept Unicode identifiers, so names, comments, docstrings and messages could all be Chinese while the syntax stays as it is. The real question is how far down to go: surface text, identifiers, or the language itself. I don't know what 象-2000 is written in, so I can't say which level is realistic yet.

On your sister's point, I don't think the aesthetic and legibility conflict. It's a strange shop with a clear sign on the door. The cyberpunk material can be the brand, since it's memorable and it's actually how you work. The homepage still needs one plain sentence, one first thing to try, and an email address. The strangeness draws people in, and the sign tells them what to do once they're there.
